reason: The myoblasts must fuse before they can form a multinucleated muscle fibre, and the fusion proteins are shown at their boundaries.
expectation: The myoblasts will join into a long cell containing multiple nuclei.

effect: The myoblasts fused and matured into a fibre with sliding filaments; its actin grip sites remain covered.
reaction: The distinction between one fibre and its many nuclei is clear and useful.
reason: The calcium pulse is the visible signal likely to expose the grip sites and initiate pulling.
expectation: Calcium will enable actin and myosin to interact so the fibre can pull.

effect: Calcium exposed the grip sites, allowing the fibre to shorten by filament sliding; it now needs to reset.
reaction: The distinction between fibre shortening and unchanged filament length is useful.
reason: The calcium-pumping membranes should return calcium to storage so the fibre can become ready again.
expectation: Calcium will be pumped back into storage, allowing the fibre to relax.

effect: ATP-powered calcium pumping stopped pulling and left the fibre ready to respond again; the next goal is to build and attach both muscles.
reaction: The outside pull needed to lengthen the relaxed fibre is a useful distinction.
reason: The biceps sheaths have empty muscle-head spaces, so the relaxed fibre is a plausible starting component.
expectation: Muscle fibres will fill the biceps sheaths to form a muscle with tendons.

effect: The fibre needed collagen-rich matrix first, producing fascicles with enough bundles for both muscles.
reaction: The connective layers clarify the distinction between a fibre and a fascicle.
reason: The fascicles can now plausibly fill the empty biceps sheaths and connect to their tendons.
expectation: The fascicles will form a biceps muscle within the sheaths.

effect: The fascicles filled the biceps sheaths, forming a muscle with tendons; the other muscle still needs building.
reaction: The force-path inset usefully connects fibres to tendons.
reason: The fascicle result said there were enough bundles for both muscles, so I will use them in the triceps sheaths next.
expectation: The fascicles will fill the three triceps heads and form a muscle with tendons.

effect: The remaining fascicles formed the three-headed triceps with its tendon; both muscles now need attachment to the skeleton.
reaction: The different routes of the triceps heads are a useful anatomical detail.
reason: The biceps tendons should attach the muscle across the movable elbow.
expectation: The biceps will attach to the skeleton at its shoulder and radius tendon routes.

effect: The biceps is attached across the elbow; the arm assembly has an empty extensor slot for the triceps.
reaction: The two poses make the biceps’ role in elbow flexion clear.
reason: The triceps is the remaining muscle and fits the named extensor slot.
expectation: The triceps will attach across the elbow, completing the two-muscle assembly.

effect: The triceps filled the extensor slot, completing the arm assembly and showing how opposite attachment positions produce elbow extension and flexion.
reaction: The contrast between the two muscles’ pulls makes their different actions clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: The calcium and relaxation sequence was most worthwhile: the planned pictures distinguish sliding filaments from shortening filaments and show why relaxation also requires ATP.

leastWorthwhile.text: Attaching the triceps was a predictable final slot-filling step, though its result made the opposing actions clear.

surprise.text: The relaxed fibre lengthens under an outside pull rather than actively pushing itself back to length.

arbitrary.text: Trying to place a fibre directly into the biceps sheaths missed the intermediate fascicle construction. The compatibility feedback resolved it, but the need for collagen layers was not obvious from the sheaths alone.

continue.text: Yes. I would continue to see how these structural constructions connect to movement and other body systems; the muscle sequence gave useful explanations rather than just naming parts.
